input.content:
# GoodWolf Harness

Project memory and a working method for coding agents.

Every session, a coding agent starts over from whatever static notes you left it. GoodWolf lets
you work with agents on one project for weeks and pick up each morning where you stopped —
without explaining the project again, without the agent re-arguing what you settled last week,
and without losing track of yesterday's half-finished work.

It keeps your decisions, open questions and tickets as Markdown under `docs/` in your repository,
and the agent reads where things stand before it starts. Each change goes through ticket, plan,
build and verify, and by default it asks you before every commit. Its rules are yours to change,
and an update never overwrites your changes. It works in Claude Code, Codex and Cursor; its
scripts are standard-library Python.

**Try it:** clone this repository, then from your project's root ask your agent to read
`.agents/skills/harness/SKILL.md` in the clone and follow it. It installs, then asks for your test
commands and where it should stop for your yes. If your project has a `CLAUDE.md` or `AGENTS.md`,
it moves them aside and does not merge them yet, so branch first and bring over what you need by
hand. More under [Use it](#use-it).

## A morning with it

An illustration: the project is made up; the steps are what the harness does.

**You:** continue

**Agent:** Picking up from yesterday. The export endpoint landed, but one of its acceptance checks
is still open: the CSV header test was never written. Next in the queue is the import endpoint.
And your question from Tuesday — do retries need idempotency keys? — is still open; we were
leaning yes. Close out the export first?

**You:** Yes, then import.

*It writes the test, ticks the check, and plans the import. Halfway through, it stops.*

**Agent:** `docs/architecture.md` doesn't say whether an import is all-or-nothing or row by row.
I'd go all-or-nothing: a half-applied import is hard to undo. Your call?

**You:** All-or-nothing.

**Agent:** Added to `docs/architecture.md`, with the reason.

*It builds the import test-first, runs your tests, checks the result against the ticket, and
asks before committing.*

**You:** Oh — exports will need paging at some point.

**Agent:** Noted as an open question under exports. It will come up again when you next work on
exports.

*Two days later, a fresh session:*

**You:** Let's make imports row by row, it's simpler.

**Agent:** Two days ago we settled on all-or-nothing, because a half-applied import is hard to
undo. Has something changed? If so, I'll reopen it and record why.

You don't type the steps or learn the commands. The agent moves the work along and stops wherever
you have told it to ask.

## What it fixes

Things people say after a few weeks with coding agents. Spec Kit, BMAD, GSD and OpenSpec all keep
plans and decisions in your repository and check work against its criteria, and so does this. The
ones marked ✦ none of those four does by default, checked against their documentation in October
2026.

- **"Every session I explain the project again."** Each session starts by reading where the last
  one stopped: what landed, what is open, what is next. "Continue" is enough.
- **"It re-argued something we settled last week."** Decisions go into `docs/architecture.md` and
  its neighbours as you make them, with the reason. The agent reads them first, and reopens one
  only when you bring something new.
- **"I lost the thread of yesterday's work."** Work is a ticket with checkable criteria and a
  written plan, so a new session picks up at the step that was left: mid-plan, mid-build, one
  check still open.
- ✦ **"I mentioned something in passing and never saw it again."** Say "oh, also…" mid-task and
  it is written down as an open question while the work in hand carries on. It comes back when
  that topic does, with where the thinking had got to.
- ✦ **"The docs say one thing and the code another."** It knows which one is wrong. Code that
  breaks a recorded decision gets a fix; a status page that fell behind the code is regenerated
  from it; history is never edited. It shows you either before changing anything, unless you let
  it fix and report.
- **"I don't know what it decided without me."** Every step leaves a short record under `docs/`.
  You choose where it stops for your yes — before a commit, a push, the next task. Out of the box
  it asks at each.

## Who it is for, and what it costs

It is for **one person steering agents on a project that lives for months** — a long-lived
product, a large refactor, a codebase you return to between other work — where forgetting costs
more every week. It is not worth it in a prototype's first week, when there is nothing settled yet
to keep, or for one-off scripts.

Before you install, know this:

- <straw-dog question="q-0024.0002">**One person, not a team, for now.** Several developers on parallel branches would collide on ticket numbers in one shared queue, and your team's tracker can't yet take the tickets' place.</straw-dog>
- <straw-dog question="q-0027.0003">**No fast path for small work yet.** Every change is meant to go through ticket, plan, build and verify. You can tell the agent to skip that for a one-line fix, but nothing yet says when that is fine.</straw-dog>
- <straw-dog question="q-0018.0005">**Instructions, not enforcement.** Everything here is the agent following written rules, plus scripts that check the files. A model can still slip; the records make the slip visible, and the rule it missed gets reworded.</straw-dog>
- <straw-dog question="q-0018.0020.0005">**In your project, nothing forces the context to load.** The agent reads where things stand because its rules tell it to. In this repository the host's hooks hand it over automatically; an install doesn't set those hooks up yet.</straw-dog>
- <straw-dog question="q-0018.0013">**No uninstall command.** Everything it adds is files, so reverting the install commit removes the harness. What it wrote under `docs/` afterwards stays until you delete it.</straw-dog>
- **Context.** A fresh project's session starts with about 4,000 tokens of rules and skill
  descriptions. In this repository, after a month of daily use, a session reads about 21,000
  before your first message: 4,200 of rules, 2,700 of status report, and
  <straw-dog question="q-0024.0009">14,500 of work queue, most of it a history log that is being moved out of it</straw-dog>.

<straw-dog question="q-0017">What it saves has not been measured. To judge it, install it into one project and watch three things over a few weeks: whether an agent arriving cold re-decides less of what was settled, whether work survives the end of a session without you reconstructing it, and whether drift between documents and code falls rather than documents piling up.</straw-dog>

## It changes with your project

Rule files for agents rot. Rules pile up and contradict each other, the agent quietly ignores
some, and your edits get overwritten when you pull an update. Here:

- **Your changes survive updates.** Your test commands, your approval settings, and any shipped
  rule you want different go in one file, `local.rules.md`. Every install and update applies it
  last and never touches it. If you edited a shipped file by hand instead, an update stops and
  tells you rather than overwrite it.
- ✦ **A rule the agent ignored gets reworded, and the next miss shows whether that worked.** When
  you or the agent notice a rule was in place and not followed, the agent logs the miss in
  `docs/rule-failures.md`, shows you the rewording, and lands it as one commit you can review and
  revert.
- **No two copies of a rule disagree.** Each rule is written in one place and copied by a script
  into every instruction that uses it. A check fails if a copy drifts from its source; it runs at
  every install and update, and in your own checks if you add it there.
- **Your own skills get the same checks.** A guided command, `/mechanism`, walks you through adding
  one, and the scripts that check the shipped skills then check yours.
- **Anything provisional says what it waits on.** A rule that will change once an open question is
  answered names that question, and the session report tells you when the answer has landed.

What a rewording looks like, from this repository's log. On 5 October the rule for placing each
message said *call `at` where the message lands*. Fresh sessions kept filing messages under
questions that merely looked similar, and you could see it in every reply. The rule was reworded
four times that day, each time after a fresh session missed it, until it read *call `at` on the
lowest question that contains the message; one that only resembles it is not its home*, and the
next fresh sessions followed it. The harness has been built with itself for a month, over 41
sessions; its log holds 22 misses so far.

To override a shipped rule, add a section naming it. This one, from this repository, replaces the
plain symbols in the per-reply status table with emoji:

```markdown
## L6 — the glyphs are anchors

- **target** `AGENTS.md`
- **authority** the user, 2026-10-07
- **overrides** `questions/Q1`

<rule>
In this tree the table's glyphs are emoji — 📍 for the question the turn ends on, …
</rule>
```

## How it works

**When a document and the code disagree, which one is fixed.** Every written thing in the
project is one of four kinds, and the kind says which side wins.

| the document says | who is right | when they disagree | for example |
|---|---|---|---|
| what it intends to become | the document, until the code gets there | the code moves toward it; the document is done once they match | a ticket, a plan, a spec |
| what must always hold | the document, always | the code is fixed; the document changes only by a decision | the architecture, the glossary |
| what exists | the code | the document is rebuilt from the code, never edited by hand | the queue's table, a check's report |
| what happened | neither — it is past | nothing is fixed | a session record, a finished ticket |

**How the right things reach the agent.** There is no vector database and no similarity search;
what the agent reads is chosen by which question you are on. Open questions form a tree, each
under the one it is part of. When a session starts, the agent reads a status report: the open
questions you keep returning to, the ones parked until a condition that may now hold, and what
other running sessions are on. Before each reply it reads the part of the tree around the
question you are on, and follows links from there.

**The steps.** You won't type these; they are the names you will see in the agent's replies. A
session starts with `/recall`, which finds where the work stopped; `/align` settles with you
whatever needs deciding; `/conclude` writes down what the next session needs. A piece of work
moves `/ticket` → `/plan` → `/implement` → `/verify` → `/maintain`; large work is first agreed with
you as a spec and split into small tickets. `/verify` asks whether finished work keeps the
promises its ticket and plan made; `/maintain` asks whether the documents still agree with each
other and with the code. Before a big decision, `/impact` traces what a change touches in this
project, and `/discover` asks a separate agent that has not read the project how things like it
usually go wrong elsewhere.

![The session steps — /recall, /align, /conclude — joined at /align to the work steps — /ticket, /plan, /implement, /verify, /maintain](dev-skills-readme.png)

The rules are in [AGENTS.md](AGENTS.md) and every skill is under [`.agents/skills/`](.agents/skills/).

## Where it stands

**Works today**, in Claude Code, Codex and Cursor:

- Installing into a project, updating it, and checking that the installed copy is intact, with
  your own rules applied last.
- Arriving in a project that already has code: the first session after install works out with
  you what the project is, and writes its architecture, decisions and glossary from that
  conversation, deepening as the work reaches each part.
- The open-question tree, with every message placed in it before the reply.
- Each rule kept in one place, and checks on the harness's own files, run at install and update.

**Not yet:**

- <straw-dog question="q-0018.0011">The install doesn't draft an architecture and glossary by reading your code and documents; the first session builds them with you instead.</straw-dog>
- <straw-dog question="q-0018.0020.0002.0003">Updates name the files they changed, not what changed in them or what your project has to do about it.</straw-dog>
- <straw-dog question="q-0018.0018">There is no way yet to send improvements your project makes to the harness back upstream.</straw-dog>
- <straw-dog question="q-0032">Sessions see where the others stand, but nothing locks: two sessions can still edit the same file.</straw-dog>
- <straw-dog question="q-0018.0023">Other hosts — Copilot, Gemini CLI, OpenCode and the rest — aren't supported yet.</straw-dog>

## Use it

```
git clone https://github.com/dveyarangi/goodwolf-harness.git
```

From your project's root, have your coding agent read
[`.agents/skills/harness/SKILL.md`](.agents/skills/harness/SKILL.md) in the clone and follow it. It
installs the harness, reports what arrived, and sets up your project's own rules with you. The
install itself is one script you can run and read first,
`python <clone>/.agents/scripts/gw/harness.py . --install`, which writes nothing if it refuses and
says why. Updating and checking the installed copy are in the same skill.

What lands in your repository: `.agents/` (the skills, the scripts and their tests), `AGENTS.md`
(the rules every session reads), a one-line `CLAUDE.md` pointing to it, and a starting work queue
in `docs/tickets/`. `local.rules.md` and the rest of `docs/` — architecture, decisions, questions,
session notes — are written as you work. Claude Code and Cursor reach the skills through symbolic
links the install makes in each clone; on Windows, where creating one may need an elevated
prompt, it prints the command to run.

Python 3.12 or later, standard library only. [MIT licensed](LICENSE).

  check still open.
- ✦ **"I mentioned something in passing and never saw it again."** Say "oh, also…" mid-task and
  it is written down as an open question while the work in hand carries on. It comes back when
  that topic does, with where the thinking had got to.
- ✦ **"The docs say one thing and the code another."** It knows which one is wrong. Code that
  breaks a recorded decision gets a fix; a status page that fell behind the code is regenerated
  from it; history is never edited. It shows you either before changing anything, unless you let
  it fix and report.
- **"I don't know what it decided without me."** Every step leaves a short record under `docs/`.
  You choose where it stops for your yes — before a commit, a push, the next task. Out of the box
  it asks at each.

## Who it is for, and what it costs

It is for **one person steering agents on a project that lives for months** — a long-lived
product, a large refactor, a codebase you return to between other work — where forgetting costs
more every week. It is not worth it in a prototype's first week, when there is nothing settled yet
to keep, or for one-off scripts.

Before you install, know this:

- <straw-dog question="q-0024.0002">**One person, not a team, for now.** Several developers on parallel branches would collide on ticket numbers in one shared queue, and your team's tracker can't yet take the tickets' place.</straw-dog>
- <straw-dog question="q-0027.0003">**No fast path for small work yet.** Every change is meant to go through ticket, plan, build and verify. You can tell the agent to skip that for a one-line fix, but nothing yet says when that is fine.</straw-dog>
- <straw-dog question="q-0018.0005">**Instructions, not enforcement.** Everything here is the agent following written rules, plus scripts that check the files. A model can still slip; the records make the slip visible, and the rule it missed gets reworded.</straw-dog>
- <straw-dog question="q-0018.0020.0005">**In your project, nothing forces the context to load.** The agent reads where things stand because its rules tell it to. In this repository the host's hooks hand it over automatically; an install doesn't set those hooks up yet.</straw-dog>
- <straw-dog question="q-0018.0013">**No uninstall command.** Everything it adds is files, so reverting the install commit removes the harness. What it wrote under `docs/` afterwards stays until you delete it.</straw-dog>
- **Context.** A fresh project's session starts with about 4,000 tokens of rules and skill
  descriptions. In this repository, after a month of daily use, a session reads about 21,000
  before your first message: 4,200 of rules, 2,700 of status report, and
  <straw-dog question="q-0024.0009">14,500 of work queue, most of it a history log that is being moved out of it</straw-dog>.

<straw-dog question="q-0017">What it saves has not been measured. To judge it, install it into one project and watch three things over a few weeks: whether an agent arriving cold re-decides less of what was settled, whether work survives the end of a session without you reconstructing it, and whether drift between documents and code falls rather than documents piling up.</straw-dog>

## It changes with your project

Rule files for agents rot. Rules pile up and contradict each other, the agent quietly ignores
some, and your edits get overwritten when you pull an update. Here:

- **Your changes survive updates.** Your test commands, your approval settings, and any shipped
  rule you want different go in one file, `local.rules.md`. Every install and update applies it
  last and never touches it. If you edited a shipped file by hand instead, an update stops and
  tells you rather than overwrite it.
- ✦ **A rule the agent ignored gets reworded, and the next miss shows whether that worked.** When
  you or the agent notice a rule was in place and not followed, the agent logs the miss in
  `docs/rule-failures.md`, shows you the rewording, and lands it as one commit you can review and
  revert.
- **No two copies of a rule disagree.** Each rule is written in one place and copied by a script
  into every instruction that uses it. A check fails if a copy drifts from its source; it runs at
  every install and update, and in your own checks if you add it there.
- **Your own skills get the same checks.** A guided command, `/mechanism`, walks you through adding
  one, and the scripts that check the shipped skills then check yours.
- **Anything provisional says what it waits on.** A rule that will change once an open question is
  answered names that question, and the session report tells you when the answer has landed.

What a rewording looks like, from this repository's log. On 5 October the rule for placing each
message said *call `at` where the message lands*. Fresh sessions kept filing messages under
questions that merely looked similar, and you could see it in every reply. The rule was reworded
four times that day, each time after a fresh session missed it, until it read *call `at` on the
lowest question that contains the message; one that only resembles it is not its home*, and the
next fresh sessions followed it. The harness has been built with itself for a month, over 41
sessions; its log holds 22 misses so far.

To override a shipped rule, add a section naming it. This one, from this repository, replaces the
plain symbols in the per-reply status table with emoji:

```markdown
## L6 — the glyphs are anchors

- **target** `AGENTS.md`
- **authority** the user, 2026-10-07
- **overrides** `questions/Q1`

<rule>
In this tree the table's glyphs are emoji — 📍 for the question the turn ends on, …
</rule>
```

## How it works

**When a document and the code disagree, which one is fixed.** Every written thing in the
project is one of four kinds, and the kind says which side wins.

| the document says | who is right | when they disagree | for example |
|---|---|---|---|
| what it intends to become | the document, until the code gets there | the code moves toward it; the document is done once they match | a ticket, a plan, a spec |
| what must always hold | the document, always | the code is fixed; the document changes only by a decision | the architecture, the glossary |
| what exists | the code | the document is rebuilt from the code, never edited by hand | the queue's table, a check's report |
| what happened | neither — it is past | nothing is fixed | a session record, a finished ticket |

**How the right things reach the agent.** There is no vector database and no similarity search;
what the agent reads is chosen by which question you are on. Open questions form a tree, each
under the one it is part of. When a session starts, the agent reads a status report: the open
questions you keep returning to, the ones parked until a condition that may now hold, and what
other running sessions are on. Before each reply it reads the part of the tree around the
question you are on, and follows links from there.

**The steps.** You won't type these; they are the names you will see in the agent's replies. A
session starts with `/recall`, which finds where the work stopped; `/align` settles with you
whatever needs deciding; `/conclude` writes down what the next session needs. A piece of work
moves `/ticket` → `/plan` → `/implement` → `/verify` → `/maintain`; large work is first agreed with
you as a spec and split into small tickets. `/verify` asks whether finished work keeps the
promises its ticket and plan made; `/maintain` asks whether the documents still agree with each
other and with the code. Before a big decision, `/impact` traces what a change touches in this
project, and `/discover` asks a separate agent that has not read the project how things like it
usually go wrong elsewhere.

![The session steps — /recall, /align, /conclude — joined at /align to the work steps — /ticket, /plan, /implement, /verify, /maintain](dev-skills-readme.png)

The rules are in [AGENTS.md](AGENTS.md) and every skill is under [`.agents/skills/`](.agents/skills/).

## Where it stands

**Works today**, in Claude Code, Codex and Cursor:

- Installing into a project, updating it, and checking that the installed copy is intact, with
  your own rules applied last.
- Arriving in a project that already has code: the first session after install works out with
  you what the project is, and writes its architecture, decisions and glossary from that
  conversation, deepening as the work reaches each part.
- The open-question tree, with every message placed in it before the reply.
- Each rule kept in one place, and checks on the harness's own files, run at install and update.

**Not yet:**

- <straw-dog question="q-0018.0011">The install doesn't draft an architecture and glossary by reading your code and documents; the first session builds them with you instead.</straw-dog>
- <straw-dog question="q-0018.0020.0002.0003">Updates name the files they changed, not what changed in them or what your project has to do about it.</straw-dog>
- <straw-dog question="q-0018.0018">There is no way yet to send improvements your project makes to the harness back upstream.</straw-dog>
- <straw-dog question="q-0032">Sessions see where the others stand, but nothing locks: two sessions can still edit the same file.</straw-dog>
- <straw-dog question="q-0018.0023">Other hosts — Copilot, Gemini CLI, OpenCode and the rest — aren't supported yet.</straw-dog>

## Use it

```
git clone https://github.com/dveyarangi/goodwolf-harness.git
```

From your project's root, have your coding agent read
[`.agents/skills/harness/SKILL.md`](.agents/skills/harness/SKILL.md) in the clone and follow it. It
installs the harness, reports what arrived, and sets up your project's own rules with you. The
install itself is one script you can run and read first,
`python <clone>/.agents/scripts/gw/harness.py . --install`, which writes nothing if it refuses and
says why. Updating and checking the installed copy are in the same skill.

What lands in your repository: `.agents/` (the skills, the scripts and their tests), `AGENTS.md`
(the rules every session reads), a one-line `CLAUDE.md` pointing to it, and a starting work queue
in `docs/tickets/`. `local.rules.md` and the rest of `docs/` — architecture, decisions, questions,
session notes — are written as you work. Claude Code and Cursor reach the skills through symbolic
links the install makes in each clone; on Windows, where creating one may need an elevated
prompt, it prints the command to run.

Python 3.12 or later, standard library only. [MIT licensed](LICENSE).

self-reported, and that nothing checks the announced version against the file. That is an open

redundant. The announcement could also move under `debug=on`, as the turn's table did.

change to the entry file, so it bumps the contract.

# q-0031 What is the harness, said to a reader who arrives cold, and what of it does the front page carry?

- **state** open
- **struck** 0, last 2026-10-07T23:12Z

Opened 2026-10-08 when the user asked for the front page to be rethought: the page of 2026-09-26
called the harness *an institutional memory in the repository*, and the tree had since gained the
question store, the four kinds of record by source of truth, the turn placed on its question, and
the whiteboard. The user's candidate line: *persistent project cognition for stateless coding
agents: preserve architectural truth, unresolved reasoning and work state so fresh agents can
retrieve narrowly instead of repeatedly rediscovering the codebase.*

What the draft of 2026-10-08 took from it and what it refused, for the user to weigh:

- Taken: *stateless*; *unresolved reasoning* as a first-class thing kept — the store earns it, and
  the old page had no word for it; *retrieve narrowly* — the window and the tiers are exactly that.
- Refused in the draft: *cognition*, on the ground that the harness is not a memory architecture.
  **That ground was wrong** *(the user challenged it, 2026-10-08)*: the
  [discover pass](../research/discover-what-this-is.md) rated family E, a self-improving agent
  memory architecture, medium-high, and its second model rated *organizational memory for an
  ephemeral workforce* high. It is a memory architecture — of the project, not of the agent. What
  sets it apart within that family: the memory is the project's and outlives every agent, shared
  across hosts and readable by a person; retrieval is by position in the question tree, not by
  similarity; and each record carries its source of truth and so the direction of its repair,
  which makes it closer to truth maintenance than to recall. *Cognition* in the user's phrase
  reads as distributed cognition — transient agents and durable artifacts as one system — which is
  defensible; the remaining objection is only how a cold reader takes the word, and that is
  untested.
- Refused: *rediscovering the codebase*. Code is the one thing an agent recovers well; what it
  cannot recover from code is the why, the rejected, the open and the stopped. The loss the page
  names is re-deciding, re-asking and re-doing.
- Missing from the line, and kept on the page: that the records are *kept true* — the kind of each
  record fixes the direction of its repair — and that the method governs itself. Without the
  first, the page describes a docs folder.

**Two `/discover` passes of 2026-10-08**, filed whole in
[discover-recall-structure-2026-10-08](../research/discover-recall-structure-2026-10-08.md), at
the user's request. The user had struck two claims: that embeddings are what sets the recall apart
(*embeddings are already going out of use*), and that a source of truth per record replaces a
recall structure (*it does not mean there is none*). What the material bears on this question:

- **The embedding claim is narrower than either side put it.** Single-vector top-k as the only
  path is losing ground, most clearly in coding agents, where agent-driven grep and navigation are
  now the backbone. Hybrids that keep an embedding channel remain the default in the memory
  literature, and Cursor measured grep plus semantic search beating grep alone. The field's
  attention moved from *which retriever* to *who controls retrieval, and how memory is written and
  verified*. So "no embeddings" sets nothing apart. What may set the harness apart is what selects
  instead.
- **The recall structure is rich, and has several selectors.** Position: the window is a
  locality prefetch, or shelf-browsing around the current call number. Activation: the strike
  count is ACT-R's base level with no decay. Dependency: suspect entries and due straw dogs come
  back because a supporting answer moved, which is truth maintenance. Obligation: tier-1 rules
  force reads. Pull is orienteering from hubs, with grep as the last resort. Neither pass found a
  published peer for a per-message push keyed on the session's position, rather than the query,
  together with a mandatory placement before the reply. Both say this is absence of evidence.
- **The source-of-truth sort is a separate axis.** Both passes read it as reconciliation or truth
  maintenance, not as recall. The user was right: it does not stand in for recall.
- **Weaknesses both passes name, measured or from the records:** the strike count never decays,
  so old questions stay ranked; the wake grows with every session ever registered, 104 lines,
  mostly ended sessions; the queue every recall reads is 58 KB, its history line 36 KB;
  single-parent placement is where rule failure 18 struck; a wrong placement makes the next push
  wrong; nothing measures whether a pushed line was used; Cursor gets no per-message push.

**The second draft, 2026-10-08, built around what the reader gets.** The user: *two axes are not
all there is in the harness; it has to be presented as a useful tool, not as a technical
curiosity.* The draft now opens on the jobs: eight problems of working with agents over weeks,
each with what changes. Then come a real example from this tree, who it is for and who not yet,
what it costs in measured sizes, and only then how it works, with the two axes inside it. Its
evidence is the [adoption panel](../research/adoption-panel-2026-09-26.md). Its six runs came
back *not for my case* on merit, while crediting the decision model. Across the runs the readers
asked for three things: the team limit up front, cost figures, and a worked example. The
greenfield reader's *the ceremony has nothing to bite on yet* became the page's line on who it is
not for.

The first example drafted was false. It said a fresh session picked up overnight what an
afternoon align had left. The transcripts show one conversation, resumed by the host under three
ids. It was replaced by a story the records bear out: q-0024.0009 was opened on 2026-10-05 and
left with its lean. The new conversation of 2026-10-06 went for the queue's next item, came back
to that question through it, and by 2026-10-08 had turned it into a spec, five tickets and two
landed slices.

**Measured against the genre, 2026-10-08.** The [README survey](../research/readme-survey-2026-10-08.md)
found the draft out of genre in three ways. Install came last, where most peers put it in the first
third. The example was the harness's own meta-work. The mechanism sat on the front page. The
survey also found that no peer says who it is not for, or what it costs. The user decided four
things *(the user, 2026-10-08)*:

- position the page against named peers;
- tell a session from the user's seat;
- keep the honest sections, compressed;
- keep the mechanism on the front page, against the agent's proposal to move it to the glossary.

The user then struck the evidence the agent was about to position from: *the 2026-09-26 pass is
long out of date*. The positioning now rests on
[what sixteen peers can do as of 2026-10-08](../research/peer-capabilities-2026-10-08.md).
State in the repository, verification against criteria, overrides and many hosts are standard
now. What the matrix finds rare, or held by no peer, is what the page now names as the harness's

Третья версия [README.md](README.md) готова и не закоммичена. Её дважды прочитали два холодных читателя: соло-разработчик и скептичный техлид, во втором круге свежие агенты. По дороге всплыла ошибка в самой странице. Прошлые версии утверждали, что хуки подают контекст в Claude Code и Codex, но установка не переносит обвязку хуков. В установленном проекте контекст подгружается только потому, что так велят правила, и теперь страница говорит это прямо.

**Почему правило объявления версии не соломенный пес.** Строка версии существует с v1 как свидетельство, что хост доставил входной файл. Открытый вопрос о ней — что это свидетельство агент заявляет сам и никто его не сверяет — жил в записи о входном контракте, а не в хранилище вопросов. Ни один проход его не открыл, поэтому правило и не обернули. Теперь вопрос открыт как q-0025.0003 с твоей склонностью, и в теле записан путь: хук на старте мог бы сам записывать доставленную версию и сверять её. Из утреннего сценария строка убрана. (💡 *Recency for evidence, longevity for principles*)

**Что изменилось на странице:**

- **Под заголовком определение одной строкой:** «Project memory and a working method for coding agents».
- **Вступление.** Вместо «забывают всё» теперь: «каждая сессия начинается с тех статичных заметок, что вы оставили». Во втором абзаце сразу видны рабочий процесс тикет → план → сборка → проверка и то, что по умолчанию он спрашивает перед каждым коммитом.
- **«Try it» предупреждает:** существующие `CLAUDE.md` и `AGENTS.md` отодвигаются и не сливаются, поэтому сначала ветка.
- **Утро.** Новый финальный эпизод: через два дня решение держится. Агент возражает с тогдашней причиной и спрашивает, что изменилось.
- **Пункты пользы теперь про результат:** «скажи "oh, also…" посреди задачи — это записано, работа продолжается». «Decisions live in…» заменено на «решения пишутся в `docs/architecture.md` по мере принятия, с причиной».
- **«It changes with your project» начинается с боли:** файлы правил для агентов гниют. Пять пунктов про результат, и настоящий пример. 5 октября правило о том, куда класть сообщение, переформулировали четыре раза за день, пока свежие сессии не стали ему следовать[^1]. # How the front page was reviewed by outside agents — 2026-10-08

A record of what was done, kept so it can be repeated. The front page was rewritten three times
in one session on
[q-0031](../questions/q-0031-what-is-the-harness-said-to-a-reader-who-arrives-cold-and-what-of-it-does-the-front-page-carry.md).
Each round was checked by agents that knew nothing of the project. At the end the user asked
that the process be saved for future use. It is a second look at produced work, by readers other
than its author, under criteria other than the author's. That is a case of
[q-0029](../questions/q-0029-how-is-produced-work-gone-over-again-over-what-scope-by-what-criteria-by-whom-and-to-what-result.md),
and it is filed there as one. This record describes; whether it becomes a skill is the user's
decision.

## The stages, in the order that worked

Each stage ran as one or more subagents in parallel. None was given another's output.

1. **What the field is now.** Two kinds of pass, both web-only and told nothing of the project:
   - *Genre*: how the front pages of the closest peers are written — opening line, section order,
     where install appears, length, examples, comparisons, limits, cost.
     [Result](readme-survey-2026-10-08.md).
   - *Capabilities*: the same fixed questions put to every peer, from current docs and releases,
     each answer dated and given a confidence. Three or four tools per pass, four passes at once.
     [Result](peer-capabilities-2026-10-08.md).

   The page's positioning is written from these, never from an older pass. The user struck a
   claim drawn from a pass twelve days old: the field had moved in that time.
2. **What the thing is, from outside.** Two `/discover` passes on the subject itself: one reading
   the repository cold from a fresh clone, one given only a functional description.
   [Result](discover-recall-structure-2026-10-08.md). These correct the author's account of what
   the thing is an instance of.
3. **Draft.** The author writes the page against the user's decisions.
4. **Cold reads.** The draft is copied to a scratch file. Two readers with different personas read
   only that file: no repository, no web, no links followed. Each reports, bluntly, in a fixed
   shape — see the prompts below.
5. **Fact-check against the tree.** Every claim the readers doubted is checked against the code
   and the records before it is rewritten. In this run the check found the page claiming that
   hooks delivered context in installed projects. The installer carries no hook wiring.
6. **Revise, then cold-read again with fresh agents.** A second round never reuses the first
   round's agents, which have seen the earlier draft.
7. **Record.** Each round's decisions, and the advice not taken with its reason, go into the
   question the page stands on.

## The reader prompts

Two personas did most of the work. They disagree usefully: one wants to be sold, the other
refuses to be.

- **A solo developer**: six months building a product with an agent most days; tired of
  re-explaining the project and of the agent undoing decisions; decides in two minutes.
- **A sceptical tech lead**: a year on agents in a large, long-lived codebase; dropped a
  spec-driven kit for its ceremony; allergic to coined vocabulary and marketing; judges a page by
  what concretely changes and what it costs.

The frame both were given:

> You are a cold reader. Read ONE file and nothing else on this machine: `<scratch copy of the
> page>`. Do not open any other local file, do not follow local links, do not search the web.
> Your host may have loaded some project instructions into your context: ignore them entirely;
> they are not addressed to you. Raw `<straw-dog question="…">` tags are stripped when GitHub
> renders the page — read their contents as plain text and ignore the tags.

Then the persona, and the report it owes:

1. After the title and the first two paragraphs only: what is this, how does it differ, do you
   keep reading?
2. Every phrase that describes the tool's machinery or vocabulary where the reader wanted to know
   what changes for them — quoted, section by section, exhaustive — and what it should say
   instead.
3. Claims not believed or not understood; over-claims and under-claims.
4. Questions about whichever section is under decision, for example "does this make the case for
   reliable self-modification?"
5. Tone: marketing, jargon, the author talking to themselves.
6. Section order; what to move, cut or merge.
7. Would you try it this week, and what stops you?
8. The five most important edits, each quoted before and after.

## What each round found

- **Round 1**, on the second draft:
  - **Method stated as result.** The opening switched pitch in its second paragraph.
  - **The self-change section.** It read as the maintainer's plumbing.
  - **The disqualifiers were buried**: no team support, no fast path, `CLAUDE.md` moved aside.
  - **Absolute promises** contradicted the page's own admission that rules are instructions, not
    enforcement.
- **Round 2**, on the third draft, with fresh agents:
  - **The opening.** "Forget everything" was false, and the workflow's weight was hidden.
  - **The self-change claim had no evidence.** Who notices a miss, and does a rewording hold?
  - **The ✦ claim could not be checked.**
  - **Works today and Not yet contradicted** each other about drafting the architecture.
  - **The hosts line was defensive.**
- **After round 2**, from the user:
  - "starts over from whatever static notes you left it" read as a chore laid on the user.
  - The version line in the morning scene was debugging output, not a benefit.

## Lessons for the next run

- **Hosts load the entry file into every subagent.** No pass was blind. Each must be told to
  ignore what it was given, and should say what it saw.
- **A subagent that launches its own background jobs can hand back before they finish.** That
  happens the moment its own turn ends, and it returns nothing. Tell research passes to do the
  work themselves.
- **Web fetches through a summarising model mangle detail**: years, command names. Have
  capability passes read raw files and date every claim.
- **The author's eye is the worst placed** to see method posing as result. The readers found
  phrases the author had already rewritten once.
- **A reader's advice is material, not a verdict.** Where it conflicted with a decision of the
  user's, the decision stood, and the record says so.
- **Check the readers' doubts against the tree before rewriting.** One doubt exposed a false claim
  the author had carried through three drafts.

A record of what was done, kept so it can be repeated. The front page was rewritten three times
in one session on
[q-0031](../questions/q-0031-what-is-the-harness-said-to-a-reader-who-arrives-cold-and-what-of-it-does-the-front-page-carry.md).
Each round was checked by agents that knew nothing of the project. At the end the user asked
that the process be saved for future use. It is a second look at produced work, by readers other
than its author, under criteria other than the author's. That is a case of
[q-0029](../questions/q-0029-how-is-produced-work-gone-over-again-over-what-scope-by-what-criteria-by-whom-and-to-what-result.md),
and it is filed there as one. This record describes; whether it becomes a skill is the user's
decision.

## The stages, in the order that worked

Each stage ran as one or more subagents in parallel. None was given another's output.

1. **What the field is now.** Two kinds of pass, both web-only and told nothing of the project:
   - *Genre*: how the front pages of the closest peers are written — opening line, section order,
     where install appears, length, examples, comparisons, limits, cost.
     [Result](readme-survey-2026-10-08.md).
   - *Capabilities*: the same fixed questions put to every peer, from current docs and releases,
     each answer dated and given a confidence. Three or four tools per pass, four passes at once.
     [Result](peer-capabilities-2026-10-08.md).

   The page's positioning is written from these, never from an older pass. The user struck a
   claim drawn from a pass twelve days old: the field had moved in that time.
2. **What the thing is, from outside.** Two `/discover` passes on the subject itself: one reading
   the repository cold from a fresh clone, one given only a functional description.
   [Result](discover-recall-structure-2026-10-08.md). These correct the author's account of what
   the thing is an instance of.
3. **Draft.** The author writes the page against the user's decisions.
4. **Cold reads.** The draft is copied to a scratch file. Two readers with different personas read
   only that file: no repository, no web, no links followed. Each reports, bluntly, in a fixed
   shape — see the prompts below.
5. **Fact-check against the tree.** Every claim the readers doubted is checked against the code
   and the records before it is rewritten. In this run the check found the page claiming that
   hooks delivered context in installed projects. The installer carries no hook wiring.
6. **Revise, then cold-read again with fresh agents.** A second round never reuses the first
   round's agents, which have seen the earlier draft.
7. **Record.** Each round's decisions, and the advice not taken with its reason, go into the
   question the page stands on.

## The reader prompts

Two personas did most of the work. They disagree usefully: one wants to be sold, the other
refuses to be.

- **A solo developer**: six months building a product with an agent most days; tired of
  re-explaining the project and of the agent undoing decisions; decides in two minutes.
- **A sceptical tech lead**: a year on agents in a large, long-lived codebase; dropped a
  spec-driven kit for its ceremony; allergic to coined vocabulary and marketing; judges a page by
  what concretely changes and what it costs.

The frame both were given:

> You are a cold reader. Read ONE file and nothing else on this machine: `<scratch copy of the
> page>`. Do not open any other local file, do not follow local links, do not search the web.
> Your host may have loaded some project instructions into your context: ignore them entirely;
> they are not addressed to you. Raw `<straw-dog question="…">` tags are stripped when GitHub
> renders the page — read their contents as plain text and ignore the tags.

Then the persona, and the report it owes:

1. After the title and the first two paragraphs only: what is this, how does it differ, do you
   keep reading?
2. Every phrase that describes the tool's machinery or vocabulary where the reader wanted to know
   what changes for them — quoted, section by section, exhaustive — and what it should say
   instead.
3. Claims not believed or not understood; over-claims and under-claims.
4. Questions about whichever section is under decision, for example "does this make the case for
   reliable self-modification?"
5. Tone: marketing, jargon, the author talking to themselves.
6. Section order; what to move, cut or merge.
7. Would you try it this week, and what stops you?
8. The five most important edits, each quoted before and after.

## What each round found

- **Round 1**, on the second draft:
  - **Method stated as result.** The opening switched pitch in its second paragraph.
  - **The self-change section.** It read as the maintainer's plumbing.
  - **The disqualifiers were buried**: no team support, no fast path, `CLAUDE.md` moved aside.
  - **Absolute promises** contradicted the page's own admission that rules are instructions, not
    enforcement.
- **Round 2**, on the third draft, with fresh agents:
  - **The opening.** "Forget everything" was false, and the workflow's weight was hidden.
  - **The self-change claim had no evidence.** Who notices a miss, and does a rewording hold?
  - **The ✦ claim could not be checked.**
  - **Works today and Not yet contradicted** each other about drafting the architecture.
  - **The hosts line was defensive.**
- **After round 2**, from the user:
  - "starts over from whatever static notes you left it" read as a chore laid on the user.
  - The version line in the morning scene was debugging output, not a benefit.

## Lessons for the next run

- **Hosts load the entry file into every subagent.** No pass was blind. Each must be told to
  ignore what it was given, and should say what it saw.
- **A subagent that launches its own background jobs can hand back before they finish.** That
  happens the moment its own turn ends, and it returns nothing. Tell research passes to do the
  work themselves.
- **Web fetches through a summarising model mangle detail**: years, command names. Have
  capability passes read raw files and date every claim.
- **The author's eye is the worst placed** to see method posing as result. The readers found
  phrases the author had already rewritten once.
- **A reader's advice is material, not a verdict.** Where it conflicted with a decision of the
  user's, the decision stood, and the record says so.
- **Check the readers' doubts against the tree before rewriting.** One doubt exposed a false claim
  the author had carried through three drafts.

| 📍 **q-0031** · What is the harness, said to a reader who arrives cold, and what of it does the front page carry? |
|---|
| **q-0029** · How is produced work gone over again: over what scope, by what criteria, by whom, and to what result? |

Начало страницы исправлено, а процесс ревизии сохранён как воспроизводимая запись и закоммичен. README по-прежнему ждёт твоего решения.

**Начало страницы.** Теперь там написано, что агент начинает каждую новую сессию заново: код он знает, но не знает, почему тот такой, что ещё не решено и где остановилась вчерашняя работа. Обязанности оставлять заметки больше нет, и неверного «забывают всё» тоже. (💡 *A capable reader*)

**Где сохранён процесс.** Запись [front-page-review-by-outside-agents-2026-10-08.md](docs/research/front-page-review-by-outside-agents-2026-10-08.md) описывает:

- **Семь этапов по порядку.** Сначала срез поля, жанр и возможности аналогов. Потом `/discover` о самом предмете, черновик, холодные чтения, сверка с деревом, повторный круг со свежими агентами и запись решений.
- **Две роли читателей и рамку промпта.** Читатель видит только файл, ничего не открывает и не ищет. Отчёт фиксированной формы заканчивается пятью правками «было → стало».
- **Что нашёл каждый круг.**
- **Уроки.** Хост подгружает входной файл в каждого субагента. Агент, запустивший свои фоновые задачи, возвращается пустым. Фетчер с пересказом путает детали. Сомнения читателей надо сверять с деревом до переписывания: именно так нашлось ложное утверждение про хуки.

**Почему запись, а не скилл.** Это запись о том, как было сделано, а не инструкция. По правилу проекта документ информирует, но не указывает агенту, что делать. Инструкция живёт только в скилле. Ревизия внешними агентами — это повторный проход по сделанной работе, то есть случай вопроса q-0029. Я записал его туда как второй наблюдённый случай после панели приёмки 26 сентября. Отвечающий тикет [01-0030 a-second-look-is-a-pass](docs/tickets/01-0030-a-second-look-is-a-pass.md) ждёт твоей правки формы, а его проверка необходимости 6 октября не прошла. Два похожих случая — это довод за обобщение, но решать тебе. (💡 *One shape is not a class*)

| ⚖️ Decisions |
|---|
| Сделать ревизию внешними агентами скиллом сейчас, через `/mechanism`, или подождать, пока тикет 01-0030 решит, один ли это проход вместе с поддержкой и проверкой? Я бы подождал: третий случай покажет, где граница. |
| Закоммитить README в этом виде? |
| Обернуть правило объявления версии соломенным псом, привязанным к q-0025.0003, с подъёмом контракта до v43? |

# GoodWolf Harness

Project memory and a working method for coding agents.

Every new session, a coding agent starts over knowing your code but not why it is the way it is,
what is still undecided, or where yesterday's work stopped. GoodWolf lets
you work with agents on one project for weeks and pick up each morning where you stopped —
without explaining the project again, without the agent re-arguing what you settled last week,
and without losing track of yesterday's half-finished work.

It keeps your decisions, open questions and tickets as Markdown under `docs/` in your repository,
and the agent reads where things stand before it starts. Each change goes through ticket, plan,
build and verify, and by default it asks you before every commit. Its rules are yours to change,
and an update never overwrites your changes. It works in Claude Code, Codex and Cursor; its
scripts are standard-library Python.

**Try it:** clone this repository, then from your project's root ask your agent to read
`.agents/skills/harness/SKILL.md` in the clone and follow it. It installs, then asks for your test
commands and where it should stop for your yes. If your project has a `CLAUDE.md` or `AGENTS.md`,
it moves them aside and does not merge them yet, so branch first and bring over what you need by
hand. More under [Use it](#use-it).

## A morning with it

An illustration: the project is made up; the steps are what the harness does.

**Two modes, the user, 2026-10-08**, at the front-page align (q-0031). Every cold reader of the
page that day named the moved-aside `CLAUDE.md` as what stops them installing. The user: *one of
the most important candidates for work, perhaps in two modes*:

- **The harness takes over.** It replaces the project's entry file and carries the project's own
  rules into itself — into the local rules file, its facts into the glossary and architecture,
  its skills beside the shipped ones. This is the flow the
  [2026-09-21 RFC](../rfc/01-0010.0150-harness-meets-a-tree-with-a-method.md) planned: an
  inventory, then the collisions settled at `/align`.
- **The harness is added by reference.** The project's `CLAUDE.md` or `AGENTS.md` stays where it
  is and authoritative, and gains one line that imports the harness's entry file. This is
  q-0018.0020.0001.0001 "Does an install keep a project's CLAUDE.md and add one import line,
  rather than move it aside?".

The RFC predates the second mode, so the ticket needs another `/plan` pass before `/implement`.
Unsettled:

- **Which rules win** in the second mode, when the project's file and the harness's disagree.
- **What updates and checks read**, when the entry file is the project's own and no longer a
  shipped file.
- **Who chooses the mode**: the person at install, or the install from what it finds.

| 📍 **q-0031** · What is the harness, said to a reader who arrives cold, and what of it does the front page carry? |
|---|
| **q-0018.0020.0001** · How does an install meet a tree that already has a method without losing it? |

Три правки страницы внесены. Твои два режима интеграции записаны в вопрос, на который отвечает уже существующий тикет. README по-прежнему не закоммичен.

**Страница.**

- **Убрано** «and by default it asks you before every commit».
- **«a harness update never overwrites your changes»** — артикль «a», потому что перед «harness» артикль «an» не встаёт.
- **«Try it»** стал одной фразой: в своём проекте скажи агенту *install the GoodWolf Harness from https://github.com/dveyarangi/goodwolf-harness*. Агент читает README, находит раздел «Use it» и идёт по нему.
- **Предупреждение про `CLAUDE.md` и `AGENTS.md`** осталось под «Try it», но обёрнуто соломенным псом, привязанным к q-0018.0020.0001. Когда интеграция появится, строка уйдёт.

(💡 *A capable reader*)

**Интеграция с существующим входным файлом.** Под неё уже есть тикет [01-0010.0150 harness-meets-a-tree-with-a-method](docs/tickets/01-0010.0150-harness-meets-a-tree-with-a-method.md), статус Ready, с RFC от 21 сентября. Твои два режима я записал в склонность и тело вопроса q-0018.0020.0001:

- **Харнесс замещает и вбирает.** Входной файл заменяется, правила проекта уходят в локальный файл правил, факты — в глоссарий и архитектуру, скиллы встают рядом с поставляемыми. Это и есть поток, запланированный в RFC: инвентаризация, затем столкновения решаются на `/align`.

65	plans and decisions in your repository and check work against its criteria, and so does this. The
66	ones marked ✦ none of those four does by default, checked against their documentation in October
67	2026.

69	- **"Every session I explain the project again."** Each session starts by reading where the last
70	  one stopped: what landed, what is open, what is next. "Continue" is enough.
71	- **"It re-argued something we settled last week."** Decisions go into `docs/architecture.md` and
72	  its neighbours as you make them, with the reason. The agent reads them first, and reopens one
73	  only when you bring something new.

75	  written plan, so a new session picks up at the step that was left: mid-plan, mid-build, one
76	  check still open.

81	  breaks a recorded decision gets a fix; a status page that fell behind the code is regenerated
82	  from it; history is never edited. It shows you either before changing anything, unless you let
83	  it fix and report.
84	- **"I don't know what it decided without me."** Every step leaves a short record under `docs/`.
85	  You choose where it stops for your yes — before a commit, a push, the next task. Out of the box
86	  it asks at each.

92	more every week. It is not worth it in a prototype's first week, when there is nothing settled yet
93	to keep, or for one-off scripts.

To judge it, install it into one project and watch three things over a few weeks: whether an agent arriving cold re-decides less of what was settled, whether work survives the end of a session without you reconstructing it, and whether drift between documents and code falls rather than documents piling up.</straw-dog>

You don't type the steps or learn the commands. The agent moves the work along and stops wherever
you have told it to ask.

## What it fixes

Things people say after a few weeks with coding agents. Spec Kit, BMAD, GSD and OpenSpec all keep
plans and decisions in your repository and check work against its criteria, and so does this. The
ones marked ✦ none of those four does by default, checked against their documentation in October
2026.

- **"Every session I explain the project again."** Each session starts by reading where the last
  one stopped: what landed, what is open, what is next. "Continue" is enough.
- **"It re-argued something we settled last week."** Decisions go into `docs/architecture.md` and
  its neighbours as you make them, with the reason. The agent reads them first, and reopens one
  only when you bring something new.
- **"I lost the thread of yesterday's work."** Work is a ticket with checkable criteria and a
  written plan, so a new session picks up at the step that was left: mid-plan, mid-build, one
  check still open.
- ✦ **"I mentioned something in passing and never saw it again."** Say "oh, also…" mid-task and
  it is written down as an open question while the work in hand carries on. It comes back when
  that topic does, with where the thinking had got to.
- ✦ **"The docs say one thing and the code another."** It knows which one is wrong. Code that
  breaks a recorded decision gets a fix; a status page that fell behind the code is regenerated
  from it; history is never edited. It shows you either before changing anything, unless you let
  it fix and report.
- **"I don't know what it decided without me."** Every step leaves a short record under `docs/`.
  You choose where it stops for your yes — before a commit, a push, the next task. Out of the box
  it asks at each.

## Who it is for, and what it costs

It is for **one person steering agents on a project that lives for months** — a long-lived
product, a large refactor, a codebase you return to between other work — where forgetting costs
more every week. It is not worth it in a prototype's first week, when there is nothing settled yet
to keep, or for one-off scripts.

Before you install, know this:

- <straw-dog question="q-0024.0002">**One person, not a team, for now.** Several developers on parallel branches would collide on ticket numbers in one shared queue, and your team's tracker can't yet take the tickets' place.</straw-dog>
- <straw-dog question="q-0027.0003">**No fast path for small work yet.** Every change is meant to go through ticket, plan, build and verify. You can tell the agent to skip that for a one-line fix, but nothing yet says when that is fine.</straw-dog>
- <straw-dog question="q-0018.0005">**Instructions, not enforcement.** Everything here is the agent following written rules, plus scripts that check the files. A model can still slip; the records make the slip visible, and the rule it missed gets reworded.</straw-dog>
- <straw-dog question="q-0018.0020.0005">**In your project, nothing forces the context to load.** The agent reads where things stand because its rules tell it to. In this repository the host's hooks hand it over automatically; an install doesn't set those hooks up yet.</straw-dog>
- <straw-dog question="q-0018.0013">**No uninstall command.** Everything it adds is files, so reverting the install commit removes the harness. What it wrote under `docs/` afterwards stays until you delete it.</straw-dog>
- **Context.** A fresh project's session starts with about 4,000 tokens of rules and skill
  descriptions. In this repository, after a month of daily use, a session reads about 21,000
  before your first message: 4,200 of rules, 2,700 of status report, and
  <straw-dog question="q-0024.0009">14,500 of work queue, most of it a history log that is being moved out of it</straw-dog>.

<straw-dog question="q-0017">What it saves has not been measured. To judge it, install it into one project and watch three things over a few weeks: whether an agent arriving cold re-decides less of what was settled, whether work survives the end of a session without you reconstructing it, and whether drift between documents and code falls rather than documents piling up.</straw-dog>

## It changes with your project

Rule files for agents rot. Rules pile up and contradict each other, the agent quietly ignores
some, and your edits get overwritten when you pull an update. Here:

- **Your changes survive updates.** Your test commands, your approval settings, and any shipped
  rule you want different go in one file, `local.rules.md`. Every install and update applies it
  last and never touches it. If you edited a shipped file by hand instead, an update stops and
  tells you rather than overwrite it.
- ✦ **A rule the agent ignored gets reworded, and the next miss shows whether that worked.** When
  you or the agent notice a rule was in place and not followed, the agent logs the miss in
  `docs/rule-failures.md`, shows you the rewording, and lands it as one commit you can review and
  revert.
- **No two copies of a rule disagree.** Each rule is written in one place and copied by a script
  into every instruction that uses it. A check fails if a copy drifts from its source; it runs at
  every install and update, and in your own checks if you add it there.
- **Your own skills get the same checks.** A guided command, `/mechanism`, walks you through adding
  one, and the scripts that check the shipped skills then check yours.
- **Anything provisional says what it waits on.** A rule that will change once an open question is
  answered names that question, and the session report tells you when the answer has landed.

What a rewording looks like, from this repository's log. On 5 October the rule for placing each
message said *call `at` where the message lands*. Fresh sessions kept filing messages under
questions that merely looked similar, and the status line on each reply showed it. The rule was reworded
four times that day, each time after a fresh session missed it, until it read *call `at` on the
lowest question that contains the message; one that only resembles it is not its home*, and the
next fresh sessions followed it. The harness has been built with itself for a month, over 42
sessions; its log holds 22 misses so far.

| 📍 **q-0031** · What is the harness, said to a reader who arrives cold, and what of it does the front page carry? |

Сделал оба исправления. Знаков ✦ на странице больше нет, новое вынесено в отдельный раздел почти в самом верху. Пример переформулировки переписан обычными словами. README по-прежнему не закоммичен, проверки чистые.

**Раздел «What is new here».** Он стоит сразу под «Try it», до утреннего примера. Первая фраза признаёт, что Spec Kit, BMAD, GSD и OpenSpec держат планы и решения в репозитории и проверяют работу по критериям, как и мы. Затем идут четыре вещи, которых ни у одного из них нет по умолчанию, по их собственной документации на октябрь 2026:

- **Ничего упомянутого не теряется.** Каждый открытый вопрос, включая брошенное вскользь, хранится до ответа вместе с тем, до чего дошла мысль.
- **Каждое сообщение раскладывается до ответа.** Агент сначала относит сказанное к его открытому вопросу, поэтому разговор держит нить между сессиями.
- **Каждый документ говорит, какая сторона права.** Решение навязывается коду, страница статуса пересобирается из кода, история не трогается.
- **Проигнорированное правило переформулируется.** Ссылка ведёт на пример ниже.

Из «What it fixes» я убрал два пункта, которые теперь стоят в новом разделе. Там остались четыре повседневные жалобы. Это я сделал по своему суждению, ты этого не просил. (💡 *Occam*)

**Пример переформулировки.** Внутренних терминов вроде «call `at`» и «lowest question that contains» больше нет. Теперь абзац такой: одно правило велит агенту относить каждое сообщение к открытому вопросу, к которому оно принадлежит. 5 октября новые сессии раз за разом относили сообщения к вопросам, которые только звучали похоже. Каждый промах записывали и правило уточняли, четыре раза за день. В итоге оно стало звучать так: относи к самому узкому вопросу, который действительно покрывает сообщение, а не к похожему. Следующие сессии справились. (💡 *A capable reader*)

# GoodWolf Harness

Project memory and a working method for coding agents.

Every new session, a coding agent starts over knowing your code but not why it is the way it is,
what is still undecided, or where yesterday's work stopped. GoodWolf lets

and without losing track of yesterday's half-finished work.

and the agent reads where things stand before it starts. Each change goes through ticket, plan,
build and verify. Its rules are yours to change, and a harness update never overwrites your
changes. It works in Claude Code, Codex and Cursor; its scripts are standard-library Python.

**Try it:** in your project, tell your coding agent *install the GoodWolf Harness from
https://github.com/dveyarangi/goodwolf-harness*. It installs, then asks for your test commands and

content.text:
| 📍 **q-0031** · What is the harness, said to a reader who arrives cold, and what of it does the front page carry? |
|---|

Раздела «What is new here» больше нет. На его месте «What it is»: пять опор, что такое харнесс с точки зрения продукта. Сравнение с аналогами сжалось до одной строки под списком. «What it fixes» влит в первую опору. README по-прежнему не закоммичен, проверки чистые.

**Пять опор:**

- **Память о проекте, а не только о коде.** В ней решения с причинами, недостроенное с номером шага и нерешённое, вплоть до вопроса, брошенного вскользь. Здесь первые два старых пункта стали одним. Отсюда «continue» без повторных объяснений и споров. Каждое сообщение привязано к своему вопросу, поэтому замечание в сторону не сбивает работу и возвращается вместе со своей темой.
- **Способ работы, который агент ведёт сам.** Тикет с критериями, план, сборка через тесты, проверка. Агент останавливается там, где ты велел спросить.
- **Система, которая держит документацию правдивой.** Для агента документы и есть память, а устаревшая страница — ложное воспоминание, по которому он будет действовать. Поэтому дрифт считается дефектом с известным способом починки. Принципы такие:
  - каждый документ объявляет, кому подчиняется, и у любого расхождения одно верное направление починки;
  - отдельный проход поддержки идёт после каждой работы и всякий раз, когда меняется то, от чего зависит документ: он сверяет документы между собой и с кодом и чинит, сначала показав исправление;
  - каждый факт живёт в одном месте, а всё временное называет вопрос, которого ждёт.
- **Инструкции, которые становятся лучше.** Обычно на пропущенное правило отвечают тем, что повторяют его снова. Здесь промах считается ошибкой в формулировке правила: его записывают, правило переписывают, а следующий такой же случай проверяет исправление.
- **Твоё для изменения, без поломок.** Твои правила в одном файле, который обновление харнесса применяет последним и не перезаписывает. Добавленные скиллы проверяются так же, как поставляемые. Ссылка ведёт в раздел с подробностями.

(💡 *A capable reader*)

**Порядок разделов теперь такой:** What it is → A morning with it → Who it is for, and what it costs → It changes with your project → How it works → Where it stands → Use it. Второй абзац вступления я сократил до одной фразы: Markdown и скрипты в репозитории, Claude Code, Codex, Cursor. Остальное теперь в опорах.

**Небольшой повтор остался.** Опоры «Инструкции, которые становятся лучше» и «Твоё для изменения» частично повторяют раздел «It changes with your project», а таблица в «How it works» — третью опору. Я оставил так намеренно: наверху коротко, ниже подробности для тех, кому нужно. Если хочешь без повторов, раздел про изменения можно свести к примеру и образцу переопределения.

| ⚖️ Decisions |
|---|
| Закоммитить README в этом виде? |
| Поставить 01-0010.0150 кандидатом в очереди, начиная с нового `/plan` под два режима? |
| Обернуть правило объявления версии соломенным псом, привязанным к q-0025.0003, с подъёмом контракта до v43? |
| Делать ревизию внешними агентами скиллом сейчас или ждать решения по тикету 01-0030? |

## What it is

- **A memory of the project, not just of the code.** What was decided and why, what is half-built
  and at which step, and what is still undecided — down to a question you raised in passing —
  kept as files in your repository. Every session starts from it, so "continue" is enough: no
  re-explaining the project, no re-arguing what you settled, no lost thread. Each message is tied
  to the question it is about, so a side remark is noted instead of derailing the work, and comes
  back when its topic does.
- **A way of working that the agent runs itself.** Each change becomes a ticket with checkable
  criteria, gets a written plan, is built test-first, and is verified against the ticket and your
  tests. You don't type the steps. The agent stops wherever you have told it to ask — a decision,
  a commit, a push, the next task — and every step leaves a short record you can read.
- **What you decide gets built, and stays built.** A decision you make is not a note; the code is
  held to it. A plan pulls the code toward it until the work matches. A decision about the
  architecture binds the code from then on: code that drifts from it is brought back, and the
  decision is never quietly bent to fit the code. After each piece of work, and whenever something
  a decision rests on changes, a separate pass checks the code against your decisions and the
  decisions against each other, and shows you each fix before making it. A decision changes only
  when you decide again.
- **Instructions that get better.** When an agent skips a rule, the usual fix is to repeat
  yourself. Here the miss is treated as a bug in the rule's wording: it is logged, the rule is
  rewritten, and the next time the situation comes up tests the fix.
- **Yours to change, without breaking it.** Your rules and overrides live in one file that every
  harness update applies last and never overwrites, and skills you add are checked like the
  shipped ones. [Details below](#it-changes-with-your-project).

content.text:
| 📍 **q-0031** · What is the harness, said to a reader who arrives cold, and what of it does the front page carry? |
|---|

Понял: без сравнений, только принципы, как они есть. README пока не трогаю, сначала список здесь. Строку сравнения уберу, когда буду переносить.

1. **Помнит репозиторий, а не агент.** Всё, что нужно следующей сессии, лежит файлами в проекте: решения с причинами, работа на своём шаге, открытые вопросы. Записи о прошлых сессиях — это история, а не источник того, что ещё открыто.
2. **Ничто поднятое не теряется.** Каждый вопрос хранится, пока на него не ответят. Каждое сообщение относится к вопросу, о котором оно. То, к чему возвращаешься чаще, поднимается выше.
3. **Решённое обязывает.** Принятое решение держит код и дальше. Расхождение чинится в сторону решения, а решение меняется только новым решением, и только при новых доводах.
4. **Записывается несущее, остальное живёт в коде.** В документы попадает только то, нарушение чего сломает несколько частей сразу. Остальное объясняют код и комментарии, и документацией тебя не заваливают.
5. **Один факт — одно место.** Каждый факт и каждое правило записаны ровно в одном месте. Копии создаёт скрипт, и проверка ловит любое расхождение.
6. **Временное говорит, что оно временное.** Всё предварительное называет вопрос, ответа на который ждёт, и сводка на старте сообщает, когда ответ появился.
7. **Работа идёт проверяемыми шагами, а где остановиться, решаешь ты.** Тикет, план, сборка, проверка, поддержка. «Выполняет ли новая работа своё обещание» и «согласуется ли всё по-прежнему» — два разных шага. Каждая остановка для твоего «да» — переключатель.
8. **Пропущенное правило — это ошибка в его формулировке.** Промах записывается, правило переписывается, следующий такой же случай проверяет исправление.
9. **Харнесс твой, менять его безопасно.** Твои правила переживают обновления. Твои скиллы проверяются так же, как поставляемые. Сам харнесс разрабатывается собой же.

В продуктовом разделе я бы оставил 1, 2, 3, 7, 8 и 9 как главные. Пункты 4, 5 и 6 — инженерные принципы, на которых держатся 1–3, и их место в «How it works». Но 4 и есть ответ на страх «меня завалят документами», так что его можно поднять наверх. (💡 *Occam*)

| ⚖️ Decisions |
|---|
| Какие принципы идут в README и в каком порядке? Мой вариант: в «What it is» пункты 1, 2, 3, 4, 7, 8, 9; пункты 5 и 6 в «How it works». |

content.text:
| 📍 **q-0031** · What is the harness, said to a reader who arrives cold, and what of it does the front page carry? |
|---|

Нет, «помнит репозиторий, а не агент» — не принцип. Это описание того, где лежат данные, и звучит оно как пустая фраза. Мой список смешал принципы с их реализацией. Твои три стоят на уровень выше, и остальное из них следует. (💡 *A capable reader*)

1. **Самоулучшение.** Харнесс сам регистрирует свои ошибки и чинит их. Это одновременно принцип и цель. Сегодняшняя реализация — соломенный пёс: если правило было на месте, а агент ему не последовал, промах записывается, правило переписывается, а следующий такой же случай проверяет исправление. В README эта часть пойдёт обёрнутой, с привязкой к q-0026 «How does the harness amend its own rules by stated meta-rules?». Раздел Self-improvement во входном файле уже обёрнут так же.
2. **Один источник истины.** У каждого факта, решения и правила одно авторитетное место. Для каждой записи известно, какая сторона права, когда запись и код расходятся. Из этого следует то, что ты назвал смыслом: принятые решения реализуются и не размываются, инструкции не противоречат друг другу, копии создаются скриптом и проверяются.
3. **Память пространства исследования.** Хранится не только то, что решено и сделано. Хранится и то, что спрашивали, что ещё открыто, куда склонялись и что временно, вместе с вопросом, которого оно ждёт. Из этого следует, что ничего поднятое не теряется, а новая сессия продолжает исследование, а не начинает его заново.

Ниже два кандидата на тот же уровень. Возможно, они не принципы, а следствия первых трёх, поэтому решать тебе.

- **Решает человек.** Агент предлагает, человек решает. Каждое решение принимается на `/align`, а где агент останавливается, задают переключатели.
- **Записывается только несущее.** В документы попадает то, нарушение чего ломает несколько частей сразу, остальное живёт в коде. Это ответ на страх «меня завалят документами».

| ⚖️ Decisions |
|---|
| Три принципа сформулированы верно? |
| «Решает человек» и «записывается только несущее» — принципы рядом с тремя или следствия, которым место ниже? |
| Порядок в README: самоулучшение первым, раз оно ещё и цель, или память пространства исследования первой, раз это первое, что читатель ощутит? |

content.text:
| 📍 **q-0031** · What is the harness, said to a reader who arrives cold, and what of it does the front page carry? |
|---|

Да, есть ещё шесть того же уровня. Каждый держит несколько механизмов сразу. Рядом с каждым указано, где он уже действует в дереве, чтобы было видно, что это не придумано под страницу.

1. **Проверяемое вместо доверенного.** Работу проверяют, а не принимают на веру. Где видно: каждый шаг оставляет запись, объявление механизма — это утверждение, которое проверяет скрипт, версия входного файла объявляется как свидетельство доставки, а «/verify» сверяет работу с её обещаниями.
2. **Решает человек, и это видно.** Агент предлагает, человек решает. У каждого правила записано, кто и когда его принял. Где видно: каждое решение принимается на `/align`, у правил есть поле authority, остановки для «да» задаются переключателями.
3. **Метод — это инженерный продукт.** Части метода объявлены, у каждой есть владелец, они проверены, версионированы и поставляются как код. Где видно: правило «Method is mechanism work», механизмы с документом, свидетельствами и проверками, версия контракта, релизы. Самоулучшение опирается на это: чинить можно только то, что описано и проверяемо.
4. **Метод общий, проект остаётся собой.** Ядро не зависит ни от одного проекта, а свои правила проекта применяются последними и переживают обновления. Где видно: разделение ядра и экземпляра, `local.rules.md`, проверка утечек, вопрос q-0018 «How do projects share one development method without losing their own conventions?».
5. **Каждое слово, которое агент обязан прочесть, стоит денег.** Пишется только несущее, остальное живёт в коде, а правило кладётся на тот уровень, где его повод читается. Где видно: принципы «Tier is paid by every session», «A capable reader», «Occam», раздел «Document load-bearing, code&comment the rest».
6. **Обобщение и пересмотр — только по доводам.** Один случай ещё не класс. Решение пересматривается только при новых доводах. Прежде чем назвать, что это такое, спрашивают взгляд со стороны. Где видно: правила «One shape is not a class» и «Recency for evidence, longevity for principles», запрет пересматривать без новых доводов, `/discover`.

Сильнейшими я считаю 1, 3 и 4: они объясняют, почему харнессу можно доверять и почему его можно взять себе. Пункт 2 близок к 1. Пункты 5 и 6 скорее дисциплина мышления агента, чем обещание пользователю, хотя 5 отвечает на страх «меня завалят документами». К твоим трём я бы добавил «временное говорит, что оно временное», но оно, кажется, уже часть памяти пространства исследования: соломенный пёс привязан к открытому вопросу. (💡 *One shape is not a class*)

| ⚖️ Decisions |
|---|
| Какие из шести — принципы рядом с твоими тремя, а какие — следствия или дисциплина, которым место ниже? |
| «Временное говорит, что оно временное» — отдельный принцип или часть памяти пространства исследования? |
